title: Calibrating a syringe pump by gravimetry
content:
Delivered flow depends on two things: how far the drive head travels (the pump mechanics — the carriage that pushes the syringe plunger) and the syringe bore you program. Weighing the water measures only their product, so calibrate them in order — do it backwards and a mechanics error hides inside a wrong "effective diameter": Pump mechanics first (Step 1) — so the drive head moves the true distance. Syringe diameter second (Steps 2–5) — the balance then corrects the bore alone. The gravimetric part needs only an analytical balance — water weighs ~1 g/mL, so 1 mg ≈ 1 µL: 
Q_real = mass / (ρ_water · time)
D_real = D₀ · √(Q_real / Q_set)
If the balance reads more than programmed → the syringe is wider than you told the pump → increase the diameter. Two web calculators (and calibrate.py) do the math — one for the mechanics (Step 1) and one for the diameter (Steps 2–5); you just type the numbers you measured. New build? Start here. This guide assumes your pump is assembled, the firmware flashed, and the controller powered and connected. You enter values (diameter, flow, gearbox, etc.) in one of two ways — use whichever you have: on the pump's keypad/screen (settings menu), or from a computer with the serial client pump_comm.py. You do not need the metrology notes (marked optional) to follow the steps — they're just the "why". Equipment Analytical balance, 1 mg (0.001 g); 0.1 mg is even better. Dial indicator or digital caliper (0.01 mm) — to measure drive-head travel (Step 1). Syringe under test, filled with bubble-free distilled water. Parafilm + a small receiving tube (e.g. Eppendorf). Tweezers/tongs for handling calibration weights (skin oil weighs enough to matter). The syringe pump. Step 0 — Calibrate the balance (once) Place it on a stable, level table (centre the bubble with the feet); no drafts, sun or vibration. Warm it up for ≥ 1 hour powered on. Empty pan, reading 0.0. Enter external calibration (on CGOLDENWALL/JoanLab HZ-type balances: Set → menu → e-cal; it requests a standard weight, e.g. cal-200 = 200 g). Place the exact standard weight with tongs, wait, remove when prompted → returns to 0.0. Verify: place a known weight (e.g. 100 g) and check it reads correctly. Step 1 — Calibrate the pump mechanics (plunger travel) ⚙️ First, match the software to this pump. gearbox, rod (lead screw) and microstep are stored per pump and must match the physical hardware you built — set them on the keypad menu or with set_gearbox / set_rod / set_microstep. Re-check them whenever you swap pumps, or move the controller between a geared and an ungeared pump. On this lab's pumps: ungeared → gearbox 1:1; geared → gearbox 100:1; both use the T8 1-star (2 mm) rod and microstep 1/8, with the same syringe diameter. A wrong gearbox shows up below as a clean ~25× / 100× travel error, a wrong rod as ~4× (see the troubleshooting table). ➡️ Open the mechanics calculator — enter flow, time, diameter and start/end readings → expected travel, error, corrected THREADROD. First check the mechanics on their own: does the drive head move the distance it should? This is the displacement method of EURAMET CG-27 §4.3.3 (lab version: laser interferometer; workshop version: a caliper or dial indicator — exactly how a 3D-printer axis's steps/mm is calibrated). This pump has no "move N mm" command — you set a diameter and a flow and let it run, so the travel comes from flow × time: Mount a caliper or dial indicator against the drive head / carriage and zero it. Keep a syringe mounted, dispensing to waste, as in a normal run (metrology labs use a rigid glass/steel syringe with the mirror on the pusher block; a normal syringe is fine here). Set the diameter D and a flow Q and run for a few minutes — longer = smaller % error (on the keypad, or set_diameter, set_flow, set_state in pump_comm.py). The commanded travel is L_set = Q · t / (π · (D/2)²) e.g. D = 9.05 mm, Q = 3000 µL/h, t = 15 min → L_set ≈ 11.7 mm (keep units consistent; the pump's max is 6000 µL/h, and the gearbox does not change this travel). Read the actual travel L_real. Repeat 2–3× and average to shrink the reading scatter. If L_real ≈ L_set, the mechanics are good. Otherwise correct the lead-screw pitch (THREADROD, via set_threadrod): threadrod_corr = threadrod × (L_real / L_set). The firmware derives steps/mm from microstep, gearbox and threadrod, so threadrod is the knob to trim. No caliper? Even a ruler works — just run longer so the move is ~50–100 mm and the coarser reading stays a small fraction of the distance. If L_real comes out very different from L_set — a clean factor points to a wrong setting; a small % is just real tolerance or reading noise: L_real vs L_set Likely cause Fix ~25× or ~100× off Gearbox set wrong set it to the pump's real ratio (1:1 / 25:1 / 100:1) ~4× off Rod wrong (1-star = 2 mm vs 4-star = 8 mm) set rod to match the physical lead screw ~2× / 4× / 8× off, gearbox & rod correct Microstep mismatch (driver ≠ firmware) check microstep — over UART it's normally self-consistent, so this is rare small (< ~2 %) lead-screw pitch tolerance or reading noise tiny THREADROD tweak, or repeat 2–3× and average erratic / not repeatable loose coupling grub screw, binding, or missed steps tighten the coupling, check for binding, lower speed / raise motor current The web calculator flags these automatically — if the error is large it tells you which parameter to check. Step 2 — Prepare the gravimetric run Fill the syringe, purge all air (a single bubble ruins a run). Mount it in the pump. Program the nominal diameter D₀ (caliper the inner bore, or use the syringe spec) and the target flow Q_set. Let the pump drip into any waste tube until the flow is steady — we use 5 min; the first minutes clear residual bubbles and let the mechanics settle. Step 3 — Collect the output, weighed (timed collection) Prepare the collection tube first: close the empty Eppendorf, seal the top with parafilm, pierce a small hole with the sharp tip of scissors (just big enough for the capillary — the thin outlet tube from the syringe — keeps evaporation low), and stand it on a small, very light base (we cut one from packing foam — negligible mass, keeps the round-bottom tube upright on the pan). Weigh it in this final state (tube + parafilm + hole + foam base) → m_empty, or tare to zero. Then collect, without stopping the flow: with the flow already steady, move the capillary from the waste tube into the collection tube through the parafilm hole, and start the stopwatch at that instant. Collect for an exactly timed interval t. Move the capillary out, press the parafilm closed over the hole, and weigh immediately → m_full. Δm = m_full − m_empty.

1 — Caliper the bore to get the nominal diameter D₀
2 — Seal the tube top with parafilm
3 — Pierce a small hole with a scissor tip
4 — Insert the capillary through the hole
Aim for Δm ≥ 100 mg (e.g. 10 min at 1000 µL/h ≈ 167 mg → <1 % uncertainty at 1 mg). Step 4 — Compute the corrected diameter ➡️ Open the diameter calculator — Steps 2–5: type the weighed values, get the corrected diameter. 
python3 calibrate.py --d0 8.94 --qset 1000 --mass 170.5 --minutes 10 --temp 20
#   flow real (balance): 1024.8 uL/h  (+2.5 %)
#   CORRECTED DIAMETER : 9.05 mm   <- enter this on the pump
Enter D_real on the pump. Repeat one point to confirm Q_real ≈ Q_set. Step 5 — Verify linearity Repeat at at least 3 flow points — the ones you'll actually use — with 3 measurements each (e.g. 500 / 1000 / 2000 µL/h ×3), following EURAMET CG-27. The 3 repeats give the repeatability; if all points return the same D_real, the calibration is solid and flow-independent. Background (optional) Delivered flow = drive-head speed × syringe cross-section. Gravimetry sees only the product, so a wrong lead-screw pitch looks exactly like a wrong bore — that's why Step 1 (travel) comes before Step 4 (bore). Many open-hardware pumps skip the split and fold both into one "effective diameter" per pump (Wijnen & Pearce, 2014): accurate flow, but you no longer know which part was off. Mechanism cycle. A lead-screw pump's flow has a slow ripple at the screw's turn period (EURAMET CG-27). Collect over ≥ 2 full turns to average it out — it's expected, not a bubble. Practical tips (what ruins a run) Evaporation: at 1000 µL/h an open tube loses ~1 mg/min — always parafilm, and weigh immediately after capping. Weights with tongs, never fingers. Exclude the first ~5 min of each run (stabilization + bubble clearing). Record water temperature; the tool adjusts density (20 °C → 0.99821 g/mL). ±2 °C is negligible (<0.1 %). Bubbles: purge before, and if the output suddenly spikes/dips erratically, there is air in the line — stop and purge. Optional: cross-check with a flow sensor (higher precision) The balance fixes the diameter. If you also have an in-line flow sensor, the same runs let you check — and calibrate — the sensor against the balance (ground truth), then use the sensor as a continuous flow reference without weighing every time. calibrate.py reports the sensor factor if you pass --sensor-ulh <reading>. For the flow-sensor hardware, firmware and high-rate acquisition, see the Rio controller: ➡️ wenzel-lab/rio-controller (pressure/flow module). References Metrology standards & guides EURAMET, Calibration Guide No. 27 — Guidelines for the Calibration of Drug Delivery Devices and Infusion Device Analysers, v2.0 (02/2026). E. Batista (IPQ), M. Benkova (CMI), H. Bissig (METAS), O. Büker (RISE). AAMI TIR101:2021, Fluid delivery performance testing for infusion pumps. ISO 7886-2, syringe cross-sectional-area tolerances (≈1 % large, 3 % small syringes). Primary methods (peer-reviewed) E. Batista et al. (2020), "Development of an experimental setup for microflow measurement using interferometry", Flow Measurement and Instrumentation 75, 101789 — the displacement method behind §4.3.3 (mirror on the pusher block; 5000 mL/h → 1.6 nL/min, U = 0.9–2 %). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0955598620301345 H. Bissig et al. (2015), "Primary standards for measuring flow rates from 100 nL/min to 1 mL/min — gravimetric principle", Biomed. Tech. 60(4), 301–316 (METAS) — the primary gravimetric standard the guide builds on. E. Batista, R. F. Martins, V. Silvério, I. Godinho (2025), "Advancing calibration techniques for accurate micro and nanoflow measurements", Frontiers in Nanotechnology — recent review comparing gravimetric, interferometric, front-track and pending-drop methods with uncertainties. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnano.2025.1600426 Open-hardware pump calibration B. Wijnen, E. J. Hunt, G. C. Anzalone, J. M. Pearce (2014), "Open-Source Syringe Pump Library", PLoS ONE 9(9):e107216 — end-to-end "push twice, take the ratio" volumetric calibration. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0107216 Baden et al. (2024), "3D Printer-Controlled Syringe Pumps…", arXiv:2402.04354 — µsteps/µL from drivetrain geometry; Marlin M92 E + gravimetric finish. https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04354 About EURAMET / IPQ. EURAMET is the European Association of National Metrology Institutes — the body that defines SI-traceable measurement in Europe. IPQ (Instituto Português da Qualidade) is Portugal's national metrology institute; Elsa Batista (IPQ) leads both the guide and the displacement-method papers above.
